conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team members. You were admitted this morning because of recurrent low blood sugar episodes, especially after your gastric bypass. We’re planning to place a gastrostomy tube today to help manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes, I’ve been having those episodes more often. Will the tube help stop the lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. The idea is to test whether feeding directly into the stomach helps stabilize your blood sugar. If it does, it might support considering a reversal of your bypass later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that was an option. Is the procedure safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s generally safe, but like any surgery, there are risks. We started laparoscopically, but had to convert to open due to some scar tissue. We placed the tube and repaired a small colotomy we found. You’re stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember waking up in the recovery room. My belly feels sore, but I’m alert.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. You’re on a PCA pump for pain with hydromorphone. We’ll switch to oral meds soon. You’re doing well neurologically and breathing fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Your labs are stable. Blood sugar was 112 this morning, which is good. We’ll keep monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about crashing again. Can I eat anything yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’re starting you on clear liquids tomorrow. Your stomach and bowels need time to wake up after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re on a Stage 5 bariatric diet today—soft foods. Try small bites and chew well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try. My belly feels a little bloated though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. We’ll get an X-ray to check for ileus—when the bowels slow down after surgery. It’s common and usually temporary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows post-op ileus. There’s no movement of contrast through your bowels. We’ll hold oral intake for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can’t eat anything? How long will this last?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It varies. We’ll encourage walking and use of the incentive spirometer. Most people improve in a few days. We’ll repeat the X-ray to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The repeat X-ray shows no change yet. We’re still seeing distention. But no free air, so no leak. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t passed gas much. Is that part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, reduced gas and bowel movements are typical with ileus. We gave a suppository, but it didn’t work. We’ll keep supporting you and wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your abdomen is less distended this morning. You passed gas and had a small bowel movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel a bit better. Does that mean I can eat again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold off on oral intake for now. But we’re planning to start tube feedings tomorrow. That’s the goal of the G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. How does that work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll connect a feeding bag to your tube. The formula is high-protein, moderate-carb. It runs slowly through a pump, 24/7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your tube feedings today at a low rate. We’ll increase it gradually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I still take my diabetes meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue acarbose and pramlintide with meals. We’re monitoring your blood sugar every few hours to make sure it stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Blood sugars are staying between 100 and 130. No hypoglycemia. We’ll keep advancing the feeding rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I haven’t felt shaky or dizzy at all today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. White count is a bit high, but that’s expected after surgery. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been walking a little more each day. My pain is better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re on oral oxycodone now, and we’ll taper that soon. You’re also on omeprazole to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember I was on pantoprazole before. Why the switch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Omeprazole is similar and works well with your other meds. We’ll keep it for now to prevent ulcers, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re tolerating full tube feedings. Blood sugars remain stable. We’re planning to discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. How do I manage the tube at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep the feedings running 24/7. Flush the tube with 100 mL water every 8 hours. We’ll send a nurse to help you at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I have problems with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you can’t flush it, if there’s leakage, or if you have nausea, vomiting, or distention. Also check residuals before feeding—if more than 50 mL, stop and call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar? Should I check it more often?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—before and after meals, at bedtime, and if you feel shaky. We want to see if the tube feedings are helping prevent lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume all your home meds except we’ve added docusate and bisacodyl to help prevent constipation from the pain meds and tube feedings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take those. When do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see Dr. ___ in two weeks. They’ll evaluate your response to the tube and discuss next steps, possibly reversal surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hopeful this helps. I’m tired of living in fear of passing out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hopeful too. This is a big step. You’ve done really well—ambulating, no fever, pain controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your final check—vitals are stable, wound looks clean, you’re passing gas, and feedings are going well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. A little nervous, but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all instructions with you. Call if you have fever over 101.5, chest pain, vomiting, or tube issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my blood sugar drops?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check it immediately. If it’s low, stop the tube feeding and call us. We may need to adjust the rate or formula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. You handled this surgery and recovery really well. We’re discharging you home with visiting nurse support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll rest, walk daily, and follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Keep up the good work. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Any new pain or concerns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just a little sore at the incision, but it’s manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Keep using the oral pain med as needed. Avoid heavy lifting for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ll have my husband help with chores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. And remember—flush the tube every 8 hours, even if not feeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 100 mL of water. I’ve been practicing with the nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re all set. We’ll call you tomorrow to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll talk soon.
